correctness.rationale: Permissible ball centers equal B_(R-r)(0) intersect B_R((s,0)). Two critical center-circle intersections determine upper and lower exposed R-spindle arcs and supporting disks preserve the remaining original-circle arc. A complete Green-formula boundary integral yields the exact area for every feasible s. Differentiation and nested center sets prove strict invertibility. Explicit Taylor inversion gives the signed \(\delta^{4/3}\) coefficient; the terminal angle expansion gives the quadratic saturation constant. All four exact Taylor coefficients and endpoint limits were independently recomputed with verify.py. The proof is analytic; finite area intersections are only stress tests.

originality.rationale: The focal 2026 full text establishes convexity and a first-order relative-affine-area limit, but not an exact all-parameter disk area function, its second coefficient, its sign-change ratio, or the quadratic terminal saturation. Earlier floating-body and relative-surface-area texts do not imply these outward-profile claims. Targeted published-finding corpus summaries and prior locally available claims showed no equivalent coverage. Historical spindle-area formula priority uncertainty remains.
residual_risks: An unindexed or inaccessible classical planar spindle-hull paper might already contain the same exact disk-plus-point area formula or its reparameterization; this could reduce novelty even when the new higher-order classification is absent.
Closest linked published-finding corpus source pages were not accessible in full, so their assessment relies on available scientific summaries, not claims of full-text exclusion.
Generality is deliberately limited to a single Euclidean disk with \(0<r<R\); no claim for general ball-convex bodies or uniform r-up-to-R limits.

value.rationale: The Euclidean disk is the intrinsic calibration case for the recently introduced R-ball illumination operator. The result solves its full finite-parameter inverse problem, identifies both nonmatching endpoint exponents, and exhibits a sharp curvature-ratio sign transition in the first genuinely new correction beyond the known relative-affine-area leading term. These structural and asymptotic facts are motivated by studying how outward ball illumination begins and saturates, not an arbitrarily sliced numerical constant.
